transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54m
Attendees: Sam (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (CTO, HorizonPort), Ana (Eng Lead), Tom (SRE), Leah (Product)

Summary: quick discovery on p95 latency targets and throughput mapping for a chat-heavy product. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for compliance and p95 guarantees. They want a pilot to validate streaming p95 at 99th percentile across concurrent users and an apples-to-apples token/sec benchmark.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency/burst model, streaming vs non-streaming throughput, KV/prefix caching, fallback model variants, security (KMS, SSO), cost tradeoffs, pilot design

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sam Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, I'm Sam from Redwood, with me is Priya our SE.
[00:08] Marcus Lee: Hey thanks, Marcus here, CTO at HorizonPort, quick context, we run a customer support assistant, real-time streaming responses are critical for UX, aiming for p95 under 350ms for streaming completions at our expected concurrency.
[00:22] Sam Ortiz: 350ms p95 streaming, okay, that's a good number to target, do you mean end-to-end (app->client) or server-only? sometimes folks mean different things.
[00:30] Marcus Lee: server-side only, client network is separate, so server p95 for token generation.
[00:36] Ana Gomez: just to add, our peak concurrent users during flash sales is about 2.5k active sessions and we multiplex requests down to about 600 concurrent model streams, average response length 80 tokens, some longer tails to 300.
[00:50] Priya Nair: got it. two quick clarifying questions — what's your current model (open or internal), and do you need private VPC / on-prem because of data residency or is it contractual?
[00:58] Tom Baker: We run a fine-tuned open model internally now, but licensing/compliance push us to prefer a private deployment in our AWS account; SOC2 is table stakes for us and we need KMS integration.
[01:09] Leah Park: And product wants <350ms p95 for conversational latency, plus cost per 1M tokens is a gating factor.
[01:16] Sam Ortiz: Great. From experience, 350ms p95 server-only with streaming and 600 concurrent streams is ambitious but feasible with the right model and batching + KV cache. We'll want to run a token/sec benchmark.
[01:28] Marcus Lee: Can you explain the quick differences we'd see between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private for our p95 and reliability?
[01:35] Priya Nair: Short answer: Hosted gives fastest path to start and Redwood manages autoscaling, but shared pools can have noisy neighbors (we mitigate aggressively). Dedicated gives predictable throughput (you reserve GPU pools) and better tail stability — good for strict p95s. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you control over network and KMS but you manage some operational complexity. For p95 you'd likely pick Dedicated for a pilot, then move to Private if policy requires.
[02:03] Marcus Lee: For Dedicated, do you provision extra headroom for bursts (like our flash sales)?
[02:07] Priya Nair: Yes, we do configurable burst capacity and autoscaler policies. For flash events you'd do a baseline reserved capacity plus a burst slab; we can size that from traces.
[02:15] Ana Gomez: About the model — quantization helps GPU throughput a lot, what's typical impact on latency for streaming?
[02:21] Priya Nair: 8-bit quant helps throughput and reduces memory pressure; latency per token can be slightly higher on some kernels but often net lower p95 because we can run more concurrent streams and avoid queueing. We also recommend KV cache warmup and prefix caching; that can shave tens to hundreds of ms depending on prompt reuse.
[02:40] Tom Baker: Do you support fallback to smaller model variants if the primary has higher latency?
[02:44] Sam Ortiz: Yes, smart routing supports model variant fallbacks by policy — latency-first or cost-first. We can define automatic fallback to a faster quantized variant if p95 starts creeping up.
[02:55] Marcus Lee: about benchmarks — what data do you need from us?
[02:58] Priya Nair: Representative traces (one week) with timestamps, token counts, streaming/response breakpoints, plus target p95 definition and which endpoints are critical. We'll run token/sec synthetic runs and a streaming replay that simulates concurrency and tail behaviour.
[03:12] Leah Park: we can provide traces but anonymized — is that OK?
[03:15] Priya Nair: yes anonymized traces are fine. We'll ask for request/response time and approximate network latencies if possible.
[03:23] Marcus Lee: Cost is huge — can you ballpark cost difference between hosted and dedicated for our volume (projected 900M tokens/month)?
[03:30] Sam Ortiz: ballpark only — hosted will be higher per-token but lower ops overhead; dedicated with reserved capacity will lower unit costs, maybe 20-40% depending on models and utilization. We'll run a model-specific cost projection after the benchmark.
[03:45] Ana Gomez: What about p95 measurement method — do you report server-side p95 per model per region?
[03:51] Priya Nair: yes, we report token-level latencies, per-route/model p95, and provide tracing hooks. You can break down by token position, streaming lag, and per-tenant tokens.
[04:05] Tom Baker: For Private deployment, can we bring our own key management (KMS/HSM)?
[04:10] Sam Ortiz: yes, Private supports KMS and HSM integration, and the control plane can be customer-managed in VPC. We'll share our security docs.
[04:18] Marcus Lee: ok. A couple technical dives — how do you handle KV cache across sharded GPUs for long conversations?
[04:24] Priya Nair: runtime keeps distributed KV slices with efficient gather/scatter; for long conversations we use prefix cache and hot-key replication for frequent contexts to avoid cross-GPU fetches. There are tradeoffs with memory and cross-GPU bandwidth but it's been effective in practice.
[04:40] Marcus Lee: any suggestions on batching/windowing for streaming to keep latency low?
[04:44] Priya Nair: prefer continuous batching with small max-latency windows (e.g., 10-20ms window) and dynamic thresholds based on load; we also use early token flush for streaming so first bytes hit client quickly while rest continue.
[04:56] Ana Gomez: can you run a quick micro example — assume 600 concurrent streams, model produces 20 tokens/sec per stream on average, what's the token/sec throughput requirement and typical GPU count?
[05:05] Priya Nair: rough math: 600 streams * 20 tokens/sec = 12k tokens/sec sustained, peaks maybe 2x so ~24k tokens/sec. GPU capacity depends on model and quant; a modern A100-equivalent cluster can handle that with sharding and batching — but exact GPU count comes from the token/sec benchmark. We'll size for steady-state and burst.
[05:22] Tom Baker: do you do cold-start profiling? our worst p95s are after auto-scale events.
[05:27] Sam Ortiz: yes, we test cold-start latency and autoscaler warm-up policies, and can recommend pre-warming strategies or keep-alive capacity for tail protection.
[05:36] Leah Park: how much observability do we get in the console for token-level traces?
[05:40] Priya Nair: token-level traces, per-route cost, latency histograms, and alerting on regression against baseline prompts. You can upload eval prompt sets to monitor quality regressions with rollouts.
[05:52] Marcus Lee: any known gotchas for streaming exports and SDKs? we've seen jitter in client playback.
[05:57] Priya Nair: jitter often comes from client-side buffering and network; we recommend small chunk sizes and immediate first byte streaming; server-side we minimize jitter by smoothing flush intervals and aligning token boundaries. We'll share SDK notes.
[06:12] Marcus Lee: security checklist — SSO, RBAC, audit logs — are these in Hosted?
[06:17] Sam Ortiz: Hosted supports SSO + RBAC and audit logs; Private gives you direct control and long-term retention options. We can provide SOC2 artifacts and exportable audit logs.
[06:28] Ana Gomez: for the pilot, what would you suggest we start with — models and quant levels?
[06:33] Priya Nair: recommend 1) baseline full-fp model for quality baseline, 2) 8-bit quantized variant, 3) tiny low-latency variant for fallback. We'll run token/sec benchmarks on all three.
[06:45] Tom Baker: timeline for pilot?
[06:47] Sam Ortiz: we can spin up a Dedicated pilot in ~2 weeks once traces and contract terms are in place; bench runs typically take 3-5 days, then a week of streaming replay to validate p95s. So 4 weeks to a realistic readout.
[06:59] Marcus Lee: ok that's reasonable. One more — how do you ensure fairness of benchmark vs our on-prem tests? we also run microbenchmarks in-house.
[07:06] Priya Nair: we'll run the same synthetic workload and streaming replay you run, side-by-side. We'll publish raw token/sec numbers, p95 histograms, and config details (batch sizes, kernel choices). We encourage a bake-off.
[07:18] Leah Park: any initial blockers?
[07:20] Sam Ortiz: main blockers are contract + security review for Private; for Dedicated pilot it's mostly sizing and traces. We'll start with Dedicated to move fast.
[07:29] Action recap: Sam to send benchmark script and pricing; Priya to propose pilot config; HorizonPort to send traces.
[07:36] Marcus Lee: great, thanks team. We'll get the traces to you by next week.
[07:41] Sam Ortiz: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for pilot kickoff and a shared spreadsheet.

(End of transcript)
